transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-05
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Parker (Redwood AE), Mei Chen (Redwood SE), John Ramesh (Arclight Head of ML), Priya Kapoor (Arclight Eng Manager), Tom Blake (Arclight Infra)

Summary: quick discovery focused on p95 targets and throughput. Arclight is latency-sensitive for customer chat and streaming financial alerts, considering Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Requests benchmarks and security docs.

[00:00] Ethan: all right hey everyone, thanks for joining on time, i'm ethan from redwood, this is mei our se, super excited to dig in, can we do quick intros?
[00:12] John: yeah thanks, john ramesh, head of ml at arclight. we own the inference layer for our customer chat and real-time alerts.
[00:18] Priya: priya, eng manager, i run the production systems and the latency SLOs.
[00:22] Tom: tom, infra, i'll be focused on network/VPC and deployment constraints.
[00:27] Mei: nice to meet you all, i'm mei, i work on performance and inference tuning at redwood. echo ethan, thanks for the time.

[00:35] Ethan: quick agenda: understanding current stack, p95 latency targets and concurrency, streaming needs and token/sec, then map to hosted/dedicated/private options and next steps. sound good?
[00:42] John: yep.

[01:05] Priya: to kick off: overview of current stack - we're running a mix of internal models and an external API for some routing, mostly on GCP with k8s. right now our endpoint that powers chat has p95 of around 420 ms for short prompts, but that includes some pre/post processing. when token generation is heavy p95 goes up to about 1.2s.

[01:33] Mei: okay that's helpful, do you have concurrency numbers? how many simultaneous users or requests per second?
[01:40] John: production peak is about 250 concurrent realtime chats, average token generation per request ~300 tokens for long-form responses, peaks to 600 tokens. rough qps for generation is around 40 r/s sustained, bursts of 120 r/s for short windows.

[02:05] Ethan: great, so p95 target? what are you trying to hit for the new rollout?
[02:09] Priya: for the customer-facing chat we want p95 under 300 ms for prompt sizes up to 100 tokens and under 800 ms for 300-600 token responses - anything over that we start seeing drop-off in product usage.

[02:26] Tom: also worth noting we have strict data residency and want audit logs, KMS integration, and SAML SSO. for production we prefer VPC peering or private deployment if the latency gains are meaningful.

[02:44] Mei: good to know. quick callouts - streaming vs non-streaming matters a lot for perceived latency. streaming partial tokens as they are generated helps the UI appear faster even if end-to-end gen is longer. are you streaming today?
[02:56] John: yes we stream in some places, but the current provider has inconsistent chunk timing so perceived latency is jittery. we want sequential token throughput of at least 80-120 tokens/s to make it feel smooth.

[03:15] Mei: got it. for benchmarks we usually measure: cold-start p95 (first token), steady-state p95 at target concurrency, token/sec sustained per GPU with batching on, and streaming chunk latency (time to first chunk and chunk cadence).

[03:35] Ethan: quick question around models - are you standardizing on a single model family? quantization?
[03:40] John: we're using an LLaMA-family variant quantized to int8 in prod, but shippable variants might be int4 for cost. accuracy must not degrade noticeably.

[03:52] Mei: okay that helps, we can recommend quant profiles. Dedicated tends to give us more predictable throughput because you control GPU pools and kernel selection, Hosted has burstiness and multi-tenant constraints but faster onboarding. Private on-prem gives lowest network hops but heavier ops.

[04:10] Priya: we care about p95 predictability more than absolute median. spikes are what kill UX.

[04:18] Mei: totally, p95 is the right metric for UX. two follow-ups from me: sample prompts and your current latency traces so we can synthesize load, and second, do you have a trial window or pilot env constraints?

[04:32] John: we can share prompts and traces. pilot ideally in the next two weeks, we can assign a small dedicated pool if numbers look good.

[05:00] Ethan: great. let me explain typical benchmark numbers we've seen. for a 300-token generation on a gpus cluster with optimized kernels and continuous batching, a single A100-like GPU with Redwood's runtime can reach ~120-200 tokens/s in steady-state depending on quant and logits size - p95 for first token often under 80-120 ms with streaming enabled, end-to-end p95 for 300 tokens often in the 600-900 ms range for dedicated pools.

[05:40] Priya: hmm those numbers for dedicated sound promising but what's our expected concurrency to reach that tokens/s? how many GPUs?

[05:48] Mei: ballpark: for your 40 r/s sustained at 300 tokens that's 12k tokens/s total. wait - math check, 40 req/s * 300 tokens = 12k tokens/s, yes. per-GPU steady-state at 150 tokens/s implies ~80 GPUs to meet sustained load if you expect no batching improvements - but with batching and caching, effective GPUs needed drops a lot. continuous batching, prefix caching (for repeated contexts) can cut token cost by 20-40% depending on overlap.

[06:23] Tom: 80 GPUs is not realistic for our budget. what's the strategy to reduce that - batching size, smaller model variants, offloading?

[06:30] Mei: yep, three levers: batching (we tune batch windows to trade latency vs throughput), quantization (int8/int4), and model routing (smaller family for cheap paths, fallback to larger for quality-critical flows). Also caching - prefix/KV cache is huge if you have many repeated contexts, like template system messages.

[06:55] John: can you give an example of latency impact of batching? we worry about p95 getting worse when batching waits too long.

[07:02] Mei: sure - typical batching window of 5-10 ms buys you large throughput because you aggregate many small requests; on p95 that can add a small headroom but effective p95 often improves because you finish more tokens faster due to GPU throughput. we instrument per-route SLOs; you can set max batch latency and max batch size.

[07:24] Ethan: - also, for streaming we ensure first-chunk latencies are prioritized with low-latency kernels and smaller micro-batches for first-token. so streaming perceived latency is usually better than full-response latency.

[07:38] Priya: good. about private deploy - if we go VPC peering or private control plane, what is the expected network addition? will we see an extra 10-20 ms?

[07:46] Mei: depends on topology. VPC peering in the same cloud region is typically sub-ms to low-ms overhead. on-prem will depend on your network stack; in practice we've seen 2-15 ms extra compared to hosted, but the predictability is better because you control the infra.

[08:05] Tom: security checklist - SSO (SAML), audit logs, KMS for key management, SOC2 compliance, and we'd like to see data residency guarantees and optional customer-managed encryption keys. do you support HSM?

[08:19] Ethan: yes to SAML/SSO, audit logging, and KMS integrations. HSM-backed KMS can be supported in Private deployments; we'll share our SOC2 report and a compliance pack.

[08:32] John: perfect. benchmarking - can you run a pilot with a synthetic harness that mimics our 40 r/s sustained and burst 120 r/s, with prompt distributions (50% short <100 tokens, 30% medium 100-300, 20% long 300-600), and measure p95 first-token, p95 end-to-end, tokens/s per GPU, and streaming chunk cadence?

[08:55] Mei: yes we can. we'll need your prompt set and expected concurrency curve. we'll propose a 48-hour dedicated benchmark window with different configs: hosted multi-tenant, dedicated reserved pool, and private (if you can provide network access or we can run a simulator).

[09:13] Priya: for security reasons we might prefer you to run dedicated in our VPC or a private pilot; tom can share the peering details.

[09:21] Tom: yes i'll coordinate network. we'll also want detailed logs for token counts and per-token latencies.

[09:30] Ethan: note we'll instrument p95 over sliding windows and include traces. we'll also run token/sec microbenchmarks to estimate GPUs required under conservative settings.

[09:45] John: about costs - we need a rough cost estimate for dedicated to see whether it's economical vs hosted. can you give a back-of-envelope?

[09:52] Mei: rough numbers: if you need 80 GPUs raw that's expensive; with batching and caching you might reduce to say 20-30 effective GPUs. Dedicated has monthly reserved pricing with commit discounts; Hosted is pay-as-you-go but variable. we'll send a sizing spreadsheet with scenarios.

[10:10] Ethan: also consider hybrid routing - critical traffic to dedicated, less-critical to hosted to save cost. Redwood supports policy-based routing and automatic fallback.

[10:22] Priya: ok that's promising. one more technical - how do you measure p95 in streaming? is it time to first token or time to last token?

[10:30] Mei: we measure both. for perceived latency UX we track time-to-first-chunk (TTC) p95, chunk interval jitter, and end-to-end completion p95. we report all three.

[10:44] John: do you have any reference benchmarks for similar fintech customers?

[10:48] Ethan: yes, anonymized case: a payments customer with similar profile saw p95 first-token under 90 ms on dedicated and sustained token throughput of ~140 tokens/s per A100-equivalent with int8, resulting in end-to-end p95 ~750 ms for 300 tokens. we'll send anonymized docs.

[11:10] Priya: that sounds in line. about SLAs - we require latency SLOs in contract, is that offered?

[11:18] Ethan: for Dedicated and Private we can include latency SLOs as part of the SLA with remediation policies; Hosted has limited SLA guarantees on p95 but uptime is SLA'd.

[11:30] Tom: will the observability give us token-level billing and per-route latency breakdowns?

[11:35] Mei: yes, the Redwood Console has token-level cost, per-model and per-route latency, traces and sampled request logs. we can hook into your tracing tooling.

[11:48] John: regarding model variants and quantization, we need you to validate no quality regression at int4. can you run evals against our eval set?

[11:55] Mei: yes we can run A/B evals as part of the pilot and include prompt-level diffs and regressions. we'll flag any statistically significant drop.

[12:08] Ethan: ok to recap - arclight will share prompt sets, p95 traces, network contacts for peering; redwood will share sizing spreadsheet, SOC2/compliance pack, and a benchmark plan. target pilot week of 2026-04-13.

[12:22] Priya: sounds good. quick logistics - can you include an explicit test harness script or k6/curl pattern so our infra team can correlate traces?

[12:30] Mei: yes we'll share the harness and we typically use a reproducible runner with token-level logging.

[12:38] John: ok, any big unknowns? i'm still worried about cost if we need tens of GPUs.

[12:44] Mei: it's always a tradeoff; we'll present scenarios showing latency vs cost curves. often a sweet spot emerges with mixed routing + caching.

[12:55] Ethan: last thing, who will be the point of contact?

[12:58] Priya: me for engineering and john for product. tom for infra.

[13:05] Ethan: perfect. thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and benchmark plan.

[13:12] (call ends)

Notes on transcript quality: occasional auto-transcription issues - "K-V cash" instead of KV cache in a couple places, speaker overlaps near end, and some numbers may be slightly rounded.
